title: Breaking Barriers: Recognition and Response
intro: Awards, adopted ways, and restorative justice. Complete Assignment 3.1 after this lesson.

terms.def: National honours recognizing Aboriginal excellence, giving students visible counter-examples to deficit stereotypes.
Conflict resolution that mends relationships through amends rather than punishing offenders.

body: Seeing someone defy the picture knocks a chip in it, which is the theory behind the National Aboriginal Achievement Awards. Mohawk conductor John Kim Bell created the foundation in 1985, the first awards followed in 1993 as the highest honour the national Aboriginal community bestows, and the winners read like a counter-syllabus: Pearl Calahasen, first Métis woman elected to Alberta's Legislature, Frank Calder of land-claims fame, author Maria Campbell, Kainai business leader Roy Fox, actor Tina Keeper, and hockey's Jordin Tootoo, first Inuk in the NHL with Nashville in October 2003. The foundation adds about $2 million a year in scholarships, and the chapter even walks your class through nominating someone yourselves.

Mainstream Canada is also adopting Aboriginal ways rather than merely applauding them. Tripartite agreements among Ottawa, a province, and an Aboriginal government now cover self-government, treaties, health, child welfare, policing, and youth services, running on consensus where every party holds an equal voice. Dunne-za Elder Dominique Habitant names the deepest import, reconciling humankind's place on Earth through respect stretched seven generations ahead, carried by teachers and artists like Sakaw Cree educator Dale Auger and Métis singer Laura Vinson.

Restorative justice shows adoption inside the courthouse. Where European tradition sees an offender freely choosing wrong and deters with punishment, the Aboriginal tradition circuit judge John Reilly describes sees a tear in the relationships binding the community and sets out to mend it, centring victim and community needs with the offender's active remorse and reparation. Youth justice committees carry the method across Alberta, and Calgary Community Conferencing brings it into city schools, giving everyone involved a voice and letting the offender propose the fix.

Three roads now converge for Assignment 3.1: excellence made visible, ways adopted into the mainstream, and identity asserted rather than assigned. The chapter's closing essay prompt, how has Aboriginal peoples' position changed since the 1970s, is your opinion paragraph in disguise. Write 3.1 as the criteria demand: two clearly described stereotypes with their sources, then a supported opinion where every claim about perpetuation and battle rides on an example from these lessons or the theme videos.

example.title: Assignment due now
example.text: Draft 3.1 in three moves: stereotype one with its media source, stereotype two with its media source, then your supported opinion answering both perpetuation and battle. One breaker, awards, adoption, or humour, must appear in the opinion.

check.prompt: Name two different ways barriers fall, with one example each.
check.sample: Sample response: visible excellence through the Achievement Awards, such as Calahasen or Tootoo, and mainstream adoption of Aboriginal ways, such as tripartite consensus or restorative justice in schools.

title: Reserve Life: Draw and Drag
intro: Why reserves pull people home and push them away, in numbers. Begin the Attawapiskat report here.

terms.def: Land set aside under treaty or law for a First Nation's use, where services, housing, and infrastructure decide daily life quality.
The Indian Act rule exempting on-reserve personal property, including on-reserve employment income, from tax.

body: The draw is belonging. Extended family close by, Elders guiding, neighbours helping starting-out families, pride in language and tradition, like the Alexis First Nation powwow, plus a freer rural pace with fishing, hunting, and trapping near at hand and ceremonies under open sky. Children roam wider, parents who left sometimes return so their kids can root, on-reserve schools teach culture and language early, and practical help follows: Elder power bills paid, rent-free or low-rent housing, and on-reserve jobs more culturally safe than mainstream ones.

Resource wealth tests that belonging. Mikisew Cree businessman Dave Tuccaro, Top 40 under 40 with eight companies, points to hundreds of millions in northern diamonds and oil sands business, and deals like EnCana with Saddle Lake keep multiplying. But Hobbema's sudden money pulled members from tradition until former chief Robert Smallboy led about 125 people to a Nordegg foothills camp in 1968 to live by hunting, fishing, and trapping again. Alberta reserves now manage carefully: Shell and Fort McKay's 400 residents plan education, jobs, culture, and infrastructure together, and the Siksika Development Corporation, founded 1995, diversifies oil and gas revenue into businesses and an industrial park, plus the $29 million First Nation-owned Blackfoot Crossing park.

Tax status sharpens every money question. Section 87 of the Indian Act exempts an Indian's on-reserve personal property from tax, including employment income for status members living and working on reserve most of the time, though settled claims have changed a few nations' status. Leaders root the right in treaties, not the Act, which Mikisew member Gordon Benoit tested by claiming Treaty 8 exempted his off-reserve income, citing commissioners who promised the treaty did not open the way to any tax. He lost at the Federal Court of Appeal in 2003 and was denied further appeal in 2004.

The drag is services and scale. Closeness curdles into lost privacy and substance peer pressure, and small size means fewer jobs and thinner schools, some struggling even with repairs, let alone post-secondary range. Ottawa aims to match mainstream basic services, yet in 2000 some reserves still lacked water and sewer, 10 percent of First Nations communities had no electricity, and 12 percent had no year-round road. Add housing shortages, crime and division, and reserves running on 80 percent or more grants and assistance, and leaving to chase opportunity makes sense. Open your Attawapiskat evidence table now: water, sewer, road, housing, schooling, and for each, who controls it.

example.title: Report starts here
example.text: Open the Attawapiskat videos and note every service failure or success against this lesson's list: water, sewer, road, housing, schooling. That table becomes your report's evidence.

check.prompt: Why do services decide so much of reserve life quality?
check.sample: Sample response: water, sewer, power, roads, housing, and schooling shape health and opportunity daily, and the 2000 gaps, plus grant dependence over 80 percent on some reserves, show what happens when communities cannot control delivery.

title: Running Their Own Show
intro: Self-government rising, languages adapting, and Métis and Inuit parallels.

terms.def: A community exercising control over its own affairs, from local programs to language and schooling.
Keeping languages alive by coining new words and carrying them into schools and daily use.

body: Control is rising, unevenly. Land-claims and self-government agreements have returned powers over language, education, and economies to many communities, which mostly plan to live alongside Canada, part of it but culturally distinct, while most reserves still work under the Indian Act toward the same goal. In 2004 Minister Andy Scott blessed the direction outright: give communities the instruments to succeed on their own terms, let them make the decisions, and treat the treaties-and-claims contract as the country's big piece of unfinished business.

New powers meet new problems, the urban kind arriving by satellite dish. Reserves now fight mine and farm pollution in land and water, prairie youth gangs feeding on alienation, and television beaming outside values at children. Self-government is the chapter's answer because only community control can respond in culturally appropriate ways, the same logic that will carry the urban half of this theme.

Languages prove the resilience thesis daily by inventing. Blackfoot speakers watch aisaiksistto, becoming visible, on an aikkamiksimstaa, quick thinker; Cree speakers tap a kîwîpahkamâhowin pîhwâpskos, marvel at a pîwâphskos icîkaân cell phone, track a pîwâpiskatahk iron star, and type on a masinatahikan smart typewriter; Dene Sùłiné board a tsi chok hetai big boat that flies; Dunne-za laugh at a woosloozhy kyaytanee stinky wagon. Living languages coin; only dead ones borrow nothing.

Métis and Inuit communities run parallel tracks without the reserve frame. The Métis Settlements alone hold collective title plus legislated self-government, while open towns like St. Laurent, Manitoba, settled by Red River Métis after 1870 and still Michif-speaking, carry culture by majority instead, earning a 2004 Smithsonian nod. No Indian Act means no tax exemption for Métis or Inuit, but the challenges rhyme: 600 abandoned toxic sites in Inuit Nunavik, seasonal water contamination for 73 percent of northern Quebec Inuit and 34 percent Arctic-wide against 19 percent for other rural Aboriginal people, and surveyors admit reserves, excluded from that survey, run worse. Inuit land-claim benefits, post-secondary help, health care, hunting rights, follow a ten-year home-link rule, Métis hold the fewest benefits of all, Edna Elias watches television dissolve visiting customs, and even Grise Fiord, Canada's northernmost civilian settlement, now connects by satellite.

example.title: Language detective
example.text: Decode three coinages without peeking: which vehicle stinks, which star is iron, which boat flies? Then argue the lesson's thesis in one sentence: coinage proves the language lives because only speakers who think in it can pun in it.

check.prompt: How do the new words prove these languages are alive?
check.sample: Sample response: speakers invent compounds like iron star for satellite and stinky wagon for vehicle, which only happens when people think, joke, and teach in the language daily.
